pr_title: Set permissions for timestamp directory before publishing update to avoid permission denied
pr_body:

1. If this is your first time, please read our contributor guidelines: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/first-contribution.md#your-first-contribution and developer guide https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/development.md#development-guide
2. Please label this pull request according to what type of issue you are addressing, especially if this is a release targeted pull request. For reference on required PR/issue labels, read here:
https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/sig-release/release.md#issuepr-kind-label
3. Ensure you have added or ran the appropriate tests for your PR: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/sig-testing/testing.md
4. If you want *faster* PR reviews, read how: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md#best-practices-for-faster-reviews
5. If the PR is unfinished, see how to mark it: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md#marking-unfinished-pull-requests
-->

#### What type of PR is this?

<!--
Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug
/kind cleanup
/kind documentation
/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This change fixes a race condition that was caused by setting the file owner, group and mode non-atomically, after the updated files had been published.
    
Users who were running non-root containers, without GID 0 permissions were getting intermittent `permission denied` errors if accessing the files during update, when they had removed read permissions from other users by setting `defaultMode: 0440` or similar and relied on `fsGroup` permissions for reading. This impacts secret and configmap volumes, and service account tokens on projected volumes.

This bug makes the system susceptible to a race condition and causes hard-to-troubleshoot intermittent failure of the application since the files likely have mandatory data for the application to function normally, such as TLS credentials. Applications are not likely prepared to retry opening the files several times since permission issues are not usually intermittent.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
<!--
*Automatically closes linked issue when PR is merged.
Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.
_If PR is about `failing-tests or flakes`, please post the related issues/tests in a comment and do not use `Fixes`_*
-->
Fixes #114461

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Following repository contains manual test procedure to reproduce the fault https://github.com/tsaarni/kubernetes-secret-race.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
<!--
If no, just write "NONE" in the release-note block below.
If yes, a release note is required:
Enter your extended release note in the block below. If the PR requires additional action from users switching to the new release, include the string "action required".

For more information on release notes see: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/release-notes.md
-->
```release-note
Fixed file permission issues that happened during update of Secret/ConfigMap/projected volume when fsGroup is used. The problem caused a race condition where application gets intermittent permission denied error when reading files that were just updated, before the correct permissions were applied.
```

> Please check the unit test failure.

Done! 

Since the PR proposes setting the final mode bits already in the payload struct, I now have changed the test to check for `0640`. This is the actual permission that has always been applied to files on disk - so no change from that perspective.  

Since the test case does not check for actual file permissions on disk, but instead only tests the payload struct, it checked for `0600` previously even though it was later overwritten with `0640` by `SetVolumeOwnership()` (this call is not included in the unit test).

/retest

There was a timeout in [TestCreateHealthcheck/timeouts_if_response_time_higher_than_custom_timeout](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/114464/pull-kubernetes-unit/1605517783183921152) which might be a flake. Running again.

> It feels like the real problem is that we finish the atomic `Write()` without calling `SetVolumeOwnership()`. Should that be done BEFORE actually publishing the contents? Maybe pass some callback into Write() ?

I was wondering that too. My thinking is: 

`SetVolumeOwnership()` fixes up permissions in the whole volume by recursively changing every file. Since we know exactly which files we create and which permissions they need, it seemed unnecessary to first create them with wrong permissions and then go through them again to correct them. 

Maybe secondary aspect is that `SetVolumeOwnership()` works on volume level. We know that the updated files are in the new timestamp directory. It seems bit redundant to go through the whole volume, including the old versions of the files that were already corrected during previous update, and will be removed at the last step of this update. 

Maybe there could be a new version of `SetVolumeOwnership()` that only touches the timestamp directory, but then again: why not set the correct permissions from the beginning? Doing the latter seemed minimal and maybe also less riskier change to fix the bug.

> but then again: why not set the correct permissions from the beginning? Doing the latter seemed minimal and maybe also less riskier change to fix the bug.

issue_context.title: Reading from secret volume occasionally fails with `permission denied`
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

Reading files from secret volume fails with `permission denied` because files incorrectly have group owner GID 0 instead of given `fsGroup`.  The failure is associated to a change/update of the files in the secret. Failure happens only occasionally and if checking the volume manually after the error, the problem has disappeared and the files can be read successfully. The ownership is wrong only for a very short while. 

The problem started after applying file permissions `defaultMode: 0440` to the secret volume and the security context with `fsGroup: 10000`. The process that reads the files is NOT running with UID 0 or GID 0.

The problem may be seen as intermittent failure of the application since secrets likely have mandatory data for the application to function normally, such as TLS credentials. Applications are not likely prepared to retry opening the files several times since permission issues are not usually intermittent. 

### What did you expect to happen?

The files on secret volume mount should be readable by the process because:
* Non-root process has privileges to read files owned by group ID 10000 - setting `fsGroup: 10000` adds 10000 to supplementary group IDs of the process
* Files on secret volume should be owned by GID 10000 because `fsGroup: 10000` was set
* The files should have group read permissions set because `defaultMode: 0440` was set

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a small test application that does following

1. Watch the secret volume with inotify
2. Wait for inotify event `IN_MOVED_TO` (which indicates that secret has been updated and atomic rename has executed to replace the files with new ones)
3. Attempt to read files the on the volume
4. Print error to stdout if opening the file fails

Create manifest for the application with following properties

* Run the process as non-root and with GID not equal to 0
* Set `fsGroup` to non-zero e.g. `fsGroup: 10000`
* Set `defaultMode: 0440` for the secret volume

Deploy the application and start updating the secret periodically. Observe error messages in the application logs when kubelet does secret updates. The application needs to be fast between steps (2) and (3). The problem cannot be reproduced with a shell script. With application written in Go the failure rate is ~50%.



### Anything else we need to know?

When extending the above test application to list the contents of the volume recursively, it can be seen that at the time of the error the the volume mount directory and timestamp directory are owned by correct group (defined by `fsGroup`), but the actual secret files are unexpectedly owned by GID 0. Furthermore it can be seen that volume mount directory has setgid bit on, but timestamp directory does not.

This ownership issue is caused by a small time window between steps (1) and (2):

1. Kubelet AtomicWriter is writing the new files on timestamp directory. It exposes them to application by renaming `..data_tmp` to `..data` ([code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f63f31b9f68e87fbede9a2de24d96a672987115b/pkg/volume/secret/secret.go#L247))
2. Kubelet calls `lchown()` recursively to change owner of all files according to `fsGroup` ([code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f63f31b9f68e87fbede9a2de24d96a672987115b/pkg/volume/secret/secret.go#L253))

There is a race condition when application attempts to read the updated files between these two steps. 

Application will fail reading the files if it is not running with GID 0 itself. Since the timestamp directory does not have `setgid` flag set ([code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f63f31b9f68e87fbede9a2de24d96a672987115b/pkg/volume/util/atomic_writer.go#L371)) the files created at step (1) will be owned by GID 0 until step (2) where they become owned by GID set in `fsGroup` ([code link](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/885961cda8875cce192700fe6a32ff57ba706106/pkg/volume/volume_linux.go#L73)).

The same problem likely applies to ConfigMaps as well, since the update logic is the same.

### Kubernetes version
